reason: The provided sources contain multiple independently verified claims across different sites regarding the discovery, scale, geometry, and thickness of Saturn's rings.
story: When Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope at Saturn in 1610, he saw two mysterious bulges that he described as ears. Two years later, the bulges vanished, leaving him to wonder if Saturn had devoured its children. The rings had not disappeared; Earth had simply crossed Saturn's ring plane, turning the massive structures edge-on. In 1655, Christiaan Huygens solved the puzzle, realizing Saturn was surrounded by a thin, flat, detached ring. What makes Saturn's rings truly shocking is their scale. The main rings span tens of thousands of kilometers across space, yet they average only tens of meters in thickness—scarcely the height of a two-story building. Composed almost entirely of reflective water ice, they reflect sunlight brilliantly from above, but when viewed edge-on every 15 years, this colossal cosmic disk is so razor-thin that it completely disappears from Earth's view.
angle: Saturn's main rings span tens of thousands of miles wide yet average only tens of meters thick, making them so razor-thin that they vanish completely when viewed edge-on.

claims.claim: Galileo Galilei became the first person to observe Saturn's rings using a telescope in 1610.
Galileo could not discern the rings' true nature, initially describing Saturn as triple-bodied or having ears.
In 1612, the rings appeared to vanish from Earth's perspective during a ring plane crossing.
Galileo was mystified by the disappearance of the rings, remarking that he did not know what to say in a case so novel and unexpected.
Christiaan Huygens became the first person to propose in 1655 that Saturn was surrounded by a thin, flat ring nowhere touching the planet.
Huygens discovered Saturn's large moon Titan in 1655.
Huygens published his ring hypothesis in the 1659 book Systema Saturnium.
Giovanni Domenico Cassini discovered the major gap in the rings known as the Cassini Division.
Pierre-Simon Laplace suggested that Saturn's ring system consists of a large number of solid ringlets.
James Clerk Maxwell demonstrated that Saturn's rings cannot be solid or continuous fluid, but must consist of numerous independently orbiting small particles.
In 1850, William and George Bond observed the faint inner C Ring, also known as the Crepe Ring.
Saturn takes approximately 29.5 Earth years to complete a single orbit around the Sun.
Earth passes through Saturn's ring plane roughly every 14 to 15 years, or twice per Saturnian orbit.
When viewed edge-on during a ring plane crossing, Saturn's rings become virtually invisible from Earth.
Ground-based estimates often placed ring thickness at around 1 kilometer, but spacecraft measurements revealed the main rings are only tens of meters thick.
Saturn's rings are composed almost entirely of water ice with a tiny trace of impurities.
Pioneer 11 discovered Saturn's F Ring during its flyby in September 1979.
Cryovolcanic geysers erupting from the moon Enceladus supply the microscopic ice particles that form Saturn's E Ring.
Gravity and mass measurements by the Cassini spacecraft indicate the rings are young, likely forming between 10 million and 100 million years ago.
The next favorable triple ring plane crossing opportunity for Earth observers will occur in 2038.

disputed: Discovery date of the Cassini Division: S1 and S2 list 1675, while S3 lists 1676; a script should state 'in the mid-1670s' or attribute to Cassini without focusing on a disputed year.
Date of Maxwell's mathematical proof: S1 cites 1859, while S3 cites 1856; a script should state 'in the 1850s'.

Age of the rings: While newer Cassini data cited in S1 and S5 points to an age under 100 million years, S1 and S2 note that theoretical models historically favored an ancient primordial origin dating back over 4 billion years; a script should present the 100-million-year estimate as the modern finding from Cassini.
